challenges.name: load-profiles-evidence
challenges.title: Load profiles: what did this run actually test?
challenges.description: Two load profiles for POST /api/submissions, the endpoint that must accept 340 submissions per second on exam day within 2 s at p95. Decide what each run tested and which numbers you can compare with the target.

questions.explanation: False. ramping-vus ramps virtual users, not requests per second: target 340 means 340 concurrent loops, and each loop sends one request, waits for the response, then sleeps 1 s. One iteration takes about 0.571 + 1 = 1.571 s, so 340 VUs produce about 340 / 1.571 = 216 requests per second, which is what http_reqs shows. This is a closed model: when the API slows down, the VUs wait longer and send less, so the load drops exactly when the system struggles. To hold 340 arrivals per second whatever the latency, use an arrival-rate executor (constant-arrival-rate or ramping-arrival-rate in k6) with enough VUs allocated. The misconception is reading a VU target as a request rate.

questions.question:
Next run, same endpoint (k6 option names; check current docs):
executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate', startRate: 0, timeUnit: '1s', preAllocatedVUs: 800,
stages: [
  { duration: '5m', target: 340 },
  { duration: '15m', target: 340 },
  { duration: '2m', target: 0 },
]

Grafana panel, per minute of the run:
 minute | arrival rate | p95 submit acceptance
 1      |  34/s        | 140 ms
 3      | 170/s        | 210 ms
 5      | 306/s        | 690 ms
 6-10   | 340/s        | 1.4 s -> 1.9 s
 11-20  | 340/s        | 2.0 s -> 2.6 s (rising each minute)
 21-22  | 255/s, 85/s  | 900 ms, 160 ms
k6 end-of-test summary, whole run: http_req_duration p(95)=1.84s

Statement: "Judged against the target of 2 s at p95 for 340 submissions per second, this run fails, although the end-of-test summary reports p95 = 1.84 s."
questions.explanation: True. The end-of-test p95 mixes every request of the run: about 51,000 from the ramp-up (average 170/s for 5 minutes) and 20,400 from the ramp-down ran at lower rates and were mostly fast, and they pull the p95 under 2 s. The target is about 340/s, so the number to compare comes from the 15-minute hold only, and there p95 rises every minute and passes 2 s from minute 11. A latency that keeps rising at a constant arrival rate means a queue is growing: the system is not keeping up with 340/s. The misconception is to trust the whole-run summary of a profile that includes ramps.

challenges.name: load-profile-schedule
challenges.title: Turn a load profile into a per-second schedule
hints: At the end of second k of a stage that goes from a to b in d seconds, which fraction of the straight line have you covered, and which way does "rounded down" go when b is smaller than a?

Look at three places: where each stage gets its starting rate (the previous target, or start_rate for the first stage), whether you validate every stage before you build anything and in the listed order, and the condition for steady: a hold keeps the rate the same, and a hold at 0/s is a pause, not a steady state.

A similar stage on other numbers: from 90 down to 20 over 4 seconds the line reaches 72.5, 55, 37.5 and 20 at the end of seconds 1 to 4, so the targets are 72, 55, 37, 20. From 20 up to 90 over 4 seconds they are 37, 55, 72, 90. In Python, -17.5 rounded down is -18, while int(-17.5) is -17.
